title: False Positive
body:
Predicted positive, actually negative. A false alarm: the model claims something that is not there.

**This is a Type I error**, rate $\alpha$, and [[Type I and Type II Errors]] in [[STATISTICS]]
(MATH 2234) owns the full translation. Crying wolf when there is none.

It sits in the denominator of precision, $\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FP})$, and of
[[Specificity]], $\text{TN}/(\text{TN}+\text{FP})$. Lowering the decision threshold buys
[[Sensitivity]] by producing more of these; there is no setting that reduces both this and
[[False Negative]] at once for a fixed model and a fixed amount of data.

**On rare positives this cell wrecks precision even when the model is good.** A test with 99%
specificity applied to a population where 1 in 1000 is positive produces about ten false positives
for every true one. That is the [[Bayes Theorem]] base-rate arithmetic, arriving from the
classification side.

Which of this and [[False Negative]] is worse is a domain question, never a statistical one: a spam
filter would rather deliver junk than eat a real message, so it treats this as the cheaper error.

See [[Confusion Matrix]] for the four cells together.
